A report yesterday indicated that Apple had previously considered creating a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but later decided to abandon the plan.

Bloomberg pointed out three reasons behind this decision, one of which was a desire not to contradict the stance taken by Steve Jobs when he launched the original iPhone. However, this is almost certainly not the decisive factor…

An Apple Pencil that works with the iPhone Ultra, shorter in size, sounds like an appealing idea at first glance. The device is essentially an iPhone that can transform into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same functionality seems entirely logical.

When Samsung launched the Galaxy Note tablet-phone in 2011, it came with an S-Pen stylus. The concept at the time was to position the device as a tool that could partially replace a paper notebook, and it continued for ten years with a loyal user base until production ended in 2021.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman listed three reasons Apple ultimately abandoned the idea:

  • Placing the Pencil on the side of the device rather than the top would make it feel awkward to hold
  • It would go against Steve's view that a stylus is a clumsy substitute for the finger
  • It would leave unsightly marks on the screen

I don't think the first point would be a major consideration, since it would be perfectly possible to mount it on the top of the device instead. This would require an extremely short design, but I think it would still work well enough.

The second point doesn't convince me either. What Steve objected to back then was not the idea that smartphones could use a stylus, but rather that the models at the time had to rely on one to operate. The real breakthrough was designing the iPhone to work smoothly using fingers as well.

In any case, Steve also publicly objected to touchscreens on the Mac on the grounds of poor ergonomics, yet we still expect the upcoming MacBook Pro models to include this feature, showing that Apple is not shy about overturning the views of its co-founder.

I think what truly killed the idea was actually the third reason. The surface of a foldable screen is inevitably far thinner and more pliable than that of existing devices. Apple is reportedly hesitant to launch its first foldable iPhone precisely because of concerns about the screen's appearance and durability; if an Apple Pencil were scraping against the screen surface over time, both would inevitably suffer damage.

If Apple one day manages to solve this problem, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini designed to work with a future iPhone Ultra? Let us know in the comments.
